utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please sit down. Can you have the accused come in? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is open. I don't know where the interpreters are, but they must be in the booth, and I still want to greet them all the same because we are starting our work in this new courtroom. Can everybody hear me? Yes, I can hear everybody. Fine. Thank you very much. The accused can hear me, so can the Defence, Prosecution as well? Fine. We are going to carry on our hearing. There might be a slight problem, Mr. Prosecutor. Mr. Harmon, do you want to take the floor and tell us all about it, how we are going to organise our work, because apparently there are new problems that have cropped up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon, Counsel. Mr. President, we do not have any witnesses to call today; however, we will be presenting evidence pursuant to Rule 85A of the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, and that evidence, Mr. President and Your Honours, has been placed in front of you. I will describe to Your Honours the binders that have been placed in front of you, there are two binders, and perhaps counsel for the Defence could be given their binders, then I can proceed and orient them through these exhibits as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, have you received this binder, or Mr. Nobilo, have you received it? Well, maybe they can be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: They have been given to us, Mr. President. With your leave, I will retrieve them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. We seem to have so much more room in this courtroom. This might give rise to other practical problems. So, Mr. Harmon, everybody is ready, so it seems? We can start with the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The first binder is a binder that consists of an index and approximately 114 tabs, and those contain documents that both are documents that have been issued by the accused in this case and by others. I will start by, first of all, explaining to Your Honours the index that accompanies this exhibit. This index is divided into six parts, and the first upper left-hand corner tab indicates the tabbed exhibit number. The next portion of the exhibit, under "Title and Document Type," indicates what type of document this is, whether it's an order, whether it is a communiqué, whether it is a memoranda, it is indicated, and the person who has issued or authored the document is also identified. If there is a document number, it is identified as well under that particular column. The next column indicates the date and the time the document was created; and under the next column, there is a description of the document and relevant passages from the document. The next column indicates the source of the document, and the last column indicates whether or not the document should be under seal. Now, some of the documents, Mr. President, have been translated into French and others, unfortunately, have not been and will be submitted to translation. Where there is a French translation available, I will indicate to Your Honours whether such a translation exists. Now, generally these documents have been indexed in a way that divides them into categories. Documents 1 through 44 generally involve a category dealing with independent units in command and control. These documents generally, in all of the categories, have been placed in date order. There are some exceptions. Documents 45 through 54 deal with combat in and around the 16th, 17th, 18th, 19th, and 20th of April. Documents 55 through 60 deal with Ahmici. Documents 61 through 68 deal with the accused's ability to appoint and dismiss HVO personnel. Documents 69 through 77 deal with the accused's ability to sentence, arrest, and punish persons under his command and control. Documents 78 through 92 generally are organised to show the ability to communicate within the Central Bosnia operation zone, so it will cover communications. Documents 93 through 103 deal with propaganda and disinformation. Documents 104 through 108 deal with training, and documents 109 through 114 are miscellaneous documents. Then, Mr. President, there is another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just one question -- sorry if I didn't pay enough attention to what you were saying. Have any of these documents been tendered already into evidence or are they all new?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, some of them have been tendered into evidence before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, there is a second binder as well, and Binder 2 consists of three publications. The first publication, Mr. President and Your Honours, is a publication which will be identified as "Three Years of Military Police," and this is a monograph about three years of HVO military police history published by the Military Police Administration from the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in 1995, and this document contains various articles that were submitted by important people of rank who were in the military police. Some of the names Your Honours will recognise by virtue of having heard their names mentioned in the course of this trial. Now, this binder consists of an index, and in respect of the index for Three Years of Military History, it is divided again into sections. It indicates, on the left-hand column, the author and the title of the document; under the next column, it indicates in English the title of the document itself, the article; and under section B it indicates whether the particular article has been translated into French. Unfortunately, not all of the articles have been translated into French, but those that have will be indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As you know, I am not a master of English, but I see "unavailable" quite a few times, so I assume that a lot of documents have not yet been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct. They will be submitted and they will be available to the Chamber at the conclusion of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, under tab 2 of this second exhibit, 457, there is a report on the work for 1992 that was prepared by the HVO, and similarly, under tab 3, there is a report on the work for 1993 that was also prepared by the HVO. French and English translations appear for both of those works. What I propose to do, Mr. President, and Your Honours, is to take you through some of these documents, and I will refer to them and indicate to you portions of those documents that I believe are important, but I would like to say at the beginning of this presentation, it is important that all of the documents be read in total, both the document itself in its entirety and the documents in respect of other documents, so that proper context can be put on these documents. These documents are being introduced for illustration purposes. So if we could, Mr. President, turn to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned friend for interrupting, but just so there is no waiver of any objections construed by our silence, I wanted to note that there appear to be documents in these binders which would not be admissible under the Court's ruling on authenticity of documents; namely, the index, for example, reflects -- this is the index to the first binder -- that most of these documents just -- again, I am roughly estimating by thumbing through the index -- came from the BH government, at least many of them came from the BH government, and that is the identified source. But they are not documents of the BH government. They are, for example, purported HVO orders or HVO documents which, obviously, were somehow obtained by -- if they are true and genuine -- obtained by the BH government, and that we don't know. To learn that, we would have to have a witness who could say the circumstances under which the documents were obtained and so forth. I also note, for example, in Exhibit 56, it's a letter from Colonel Stewart, and obviously Colonel Stewart -- maybe he is still coming in this case to testify, but perhaps not. So we simply note that we have a question whether these documents would be admissible under the Court's prior ruling, and if they are to be admitted, if that ruling has been modified and, of course, will it be applied -- whatever the new rule might be, will it be applied in an even-handed manner to both sides. We would presume so. We, of course, will read the documents, and if we have specific objections, we will make them in writing, but I wanted to note those general observations at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: (translation interrupts) ... these documents, we are prepared to go further to identify, on any particular document, the manner in which it was obtained, who obtained it, and satisfy this Court and satisfy Defence counsel as to how we obtained and how we recovered these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do understand what Mr. Hayman said because he referred back to a ruling; however, that ruling dealt with witnesses and an exhibit tendered to a witness to know whether the witness was able to identify the document or not. We're dealing with something different here. We are having documents presented to us. I suggest they should be admitted with the proviso that you are presently formulating. If, after seeing the document, Mr. Hayman, you have to raise objections as to their authenticity, not as to their relevance, because that has to be ascertained by the Judges. But if you have an objection as to the authenticity, of course, the Prosecutor, when you present your case, will have to answer to your objections, and if there is a failure to answer, we shall draw the legal conclusions that seem necessary to be drawn. This is a solution I suggest to you. Whilst I have the floor, let me tell you this: Mr. Harmon, in this new courtroom, you always have the Prosecution on that bench? Because there you are standing on your feet, and it's a practical matter, because if there is an objection coming from the Defence counsel, you can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can certainly always hear Mr. Hayman object, Mr. President. There is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. Just pretending you were not turning around to see him. Fine. If there's no problem, that's fine for me. Thank you. I suppose you are going to present to us those documents that seem most important to you; is that what you intend to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could invite your attention first to document number 1, tab 1, that would be 456-1, I think is the correct exhibit number, and I only invite your attention to this document because it is a document which indicates that -- it is an order from Colonel Blaskic dated the 7th of September, 1992, and it is an order to municipal headquarters to establish security and intelligence services for the area. In respect of the second tab, 456-2, this is a document which was an order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 26th of September, 1992, and it is issued pursuant to an order of the general staff, to all municipal staff commanders, to form special units for combat operations. I should add, Mr. President, there is a French translation of this particular document. The next document, Mr. President, I would like to turn your attention to, is document number 4. There is no French translation for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. I just had some practical difficulties here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am dealing with documents 1 through 44 which deal with independent units and with command and control, and I have referred Your Honours to document number 4. That is an order from Colonel Blaskic dealing with discipline and conduct and it has been issued on the 12th of November, 1992. Specifically, it has been issued to all HVO brigade commanders in the municipal headquarters of Central Bosnia operative zone, and I invite your attention to paragraph 12 of that document. In that document, and I will quote: "I prohibit the establishment of personal units in Central Bosnia operation zone. However, should there be such a unit, brigade commanders must immediately inform the superior command. Members of personal units shall be immediately disarmed, arrested, and surrendered to the competent authorities. All means shall be available to carry out this order." Now, Mr. President, if I could invite your attention to number 6, tab 6? This, Mr. President, is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic for full combat readiness of all HVO formations in the Central Bosnia operations zone. It was issued on the 16th of January, 1993, at 11.40 hours, and slightly above the middle of the page on the right-hand side is a list of the addressees, and Your Honour will see that this order was issued to all the formations in Central Bosnia operations zone, and then it lists a number of those organisations, Bruno Busic formation, the Ludwig Pavlovic formation, the Vitezovi formation, the Travnik Police Department, and the 4th Battalion Military Police in Vitez. Now, Mr. President, I invite your attention to tab number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can understand what problems the interpreters are confronted with because they don't have the documents; at least in the French booth, they don't have the index either. I can see that you are using your index to introduce various arguments. Would it be possible for the interpreters to have at least that index?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How many copies would we need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have a spare copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At least one for the French booth. Thank you very much. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could invite your attention now to item number 9 in the exhibit? This is an order that was issued on the 11th of February, 1993, by the chief of the HVO main staff, Milvoj Petkovic and Sefer Halilovic, the chief of the RBH Supreme Command, and it was issued to Colonel Blaskic, amongst others. What follows then, Mr. President, in items numbers 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14 are a series of orders that were issued by Colonel Blaskic pursuant to the order he had received from his superior commander. Now, if I could invite your attention to tab number 15? Tab number 15, Mr. President, is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic, and it was issued on the 13th of February, 1993, at 12.30 hours. Again, in that particular exhibit, if Your Honours turn your attention to the right-hand side, upper portion of the page, there is a list of addressees to whom this order was issued. I won't read it, but included in there is the 4th Vitez Military Police Battalion and the commander of the Vitezovi Special Purposes Units. Tab number 16, Mr. President, is another order issued by Colonel Blaskic, this time on the 17th of March, 1993, at 12.00 hours. There is a French translation of that. Again, I draw your attention to the addressees of this particular order, and Your Honours will find included in that the Vitez Military Police 4th Battalion and Your Honours will also find the Vitezovi Special Task Force. Now if we turn to tab 18? This again, Mr. President, is a -- this is an interesting document because this is conclusions made at a conference of the heads of the section for organisation and personnel matters, and Your Honours can see to whom this particular set of conclusions has been addressed. The conclusions were -- this order is signed by Colonel Blaskic, and it indicates in the second paragraph of that, and I quote: "The Ban Jelacic brigade located in Stojkovici logistic space, the SB OZ communications company, and the Vitezovi Special Purposes Unit from Vitez were not present at the conference." So it indicates, Mr. President, that there was a conference that was for matters of brigades and independent units of the Central Bosnia operation zone and that the Vitezovi were not represented at that particular conference. Now, Mr. President, if we turn to number 20, tab 20. Tab 20 is a protest, signed by Darko Kraljevic dated the 15th of April, 1993, and Your Honours will notice on this particular exhibit the second paragraph of this particular exhibit, which I will read: "The Vitezovi unit is, as the name indicates, a special unit which is in the unified system of command and control in the SB operative zone and is also responsible to its superior command for its actions." I note, I direct Your Honours' attention as well, to the seal that appears over the signature line of Darko Kraljevic, a seal which is a stamp that has "Vitezovi" on it. Now if I my direct your attention to item number 21? Item number 21 is a command that has been issued by Colonel Blaskic. I should add, Mr. President, there is a French translation of this. This command was issued on the 16th of April, 1993, at 19.40 hours. It is a command which directs the 4th Military Police Battalion to move to Vitez to enforce troops of the Viteska brigade, and I note and I draw your attention to paragraph 3, which reads: "I shall be informed of the arrival of the entire unit in Vitez so that I may issue concrete orders." Now, Mr. President, if you would turn to tab 25? This is an order, and I note, first of all, the order number in the upper left hand is 01-659-93. This was issued on the 20th of April, 1993, by General Petkovic from the main headquarters, and the addressees in this particular document are the four operative zones, one of which is the Central Bosnia operation zone. If you turn, Mr. President, and Your Honours, to item number 7 of that document, the command by General Petkovic to General Blaskic is, and I quote: "Inform all subordinate units under your command of this order once again." Now, Mr. President, if you turn to item number 26, you see a corresponding order that was issued by Colonel Blaskic as a result of the order he received from General Petkovic. That order, which is found in tab 26, is dated the 21st of April, 1993. As he was instructed to issue/inform all subordinate units under his command of the order, you will notice, Mr. President, in the upper right-hand corner of this document the addressees to whom he addresses the order. Those addressees are "HVO Brigade Command 1 through 12, independent units in Central Bosnia operative zone (4th LARD motorised division, Vitez Military Police 4th Battalion, and the Vitezovi Special Task Force)." Now, Mr. President, if I could turn to tab 32, this is an important document. This document, Mr. President, is a special report on the situation in the Central Bosnia operative zone of the HVO of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. It is dated the 7th of May, 1993. The time it was issued was at 12.30, and the author of this is Colonel Blaskic. The addressees of this particular document are the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, the head of the defence department of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and the chief of the main headquarters of HVO Croatian Defence Council, Mostar. Mr. President, there is a French translation of this, I have omitted to say. If you turn in this document toward the end of this document, unfortunately it's not paginated, but with the ERN number on the top, it's the page that is numbered 00564013. In the centre of the page of the English translation, it reads as follows: "Central Bosnia Operative Zone HVO Forces," and then it follows: "1) Strength: The following are engaged in the defence against MOS attacks: The brigades Ban Jelacic, Kiseljak, the Busovaca Nikola Subic Zrinjski Brigade, without the 3rd Bojnica Battalion, the Viteska Brigade, with the support and in conjunction with the HVO Brigade Novi Travnik, IV LTRD, MTD, parts of the IV Military Police Battalion, a battalion (60 men), the Vitezovi PN." Now, Mr. President, if you turn further into that document, and it is on page 015 of the English translation of this document, there's a conclusion. Let me read the conclusion to Your Honours. "1) Command and control function properly and all missions proceed in a planned fashion according to orders with detailed knowledge of the situation, full coordination and control." There are other parts of this document. I would urge Your Honours to read this document in full, but this is, again, dated the 7th of May, 1993. Your Honours, even though I am omitting these orders and documents, Mr. President, I would urge you to look at the addressees on all of these documents. There are a significant number of them that I have not particularly mentioned but many of which contained the Vitezovi, among others. I would like to direct your attention, Mr. President, now to item 37. This is an order of Colonel Blaskic which is dated the 17th of June, 1993 at 15.55 hours. This is an order that has been the -- I'm sorry. This, Mr. President, is the result of an order which Colonel Blaskic received from his superior officer. It indicates that due to signed agreements based on the cessation of hostilities in Bosnia - and he identifies those particular agreements - then he issues this particular order. He issues it -- again, I would direct your attention to the addressees on this list. He addresses it to all brigades and independent units, and they are identified, "Mechanised Tank Division, Light Artillery Rocket Division, 4th Military Police Battalion, Stojkovici: logistics base, Vitezovi, Tvrtko TT, Zuti, Special Purposes Units." Now, Mr. President, this is a document, the first page of this document is the English translation. There are three separate documents under tab 37. What I've just read from is the English translation of a document but there are two following documents. One is a document that has been previously identified by Henk Morsink, a witness from ECMM, that he received while he was in theatre and it is in English. Let me direct your attention to that particular document, to the distribution list of that particular document. The distribution of this particular document is as follows: All the HVO brigades, all the independent units under the command of the HVO 3rd OZ commander, and then there's a parenthesis "(MTD 4 LTRD, 4th Military Police Battalion, Vitezovi, Tvrtko 2, and Zuti)." The last document at 37 is another document that was also received by Mr. Morsink which he has identified previously. It's in the Croatian language. Now, Mr. President, very briefly if we could turn to tab 38, an order that was issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 19th of June, 1993. Again, I only direct your attention to the addressees of this particular document. The addressees include the Vitezovi special task force. Lastly, Mr. President, I would like to direct your attention to tab 41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you were referring to tab 38 and you stated the date as 19th of June. Would you direct my attention to that date, the 19th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Shahabuddeen. If one turns to the copy -- second copy which is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. The one in BSC?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, there's an English copy that Lieutenant Colonel Morsink identified. It is the one that he received. It is the one above the BCS edition. It is this document, Judge Shahabuddeen. I don't know if you can see what I'm holding up from here, but it is this particular document in tab 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In the upper left-hand corner, there's a date of June 19th, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, lastly, if I could direct your attention to tab 41, I invite your attention only to illustrate the date on this particular document, which is an order of Colonel Blaskic. It is dated the 11th of October, 1993. Again, I direct your attention to the addressees which include, amongst others, the Vitezovi and Tvrtko 2. Now, these documents are tendered, among other things, to indicate to whom Colonel Blaskic was giving his orders and instructions. If I could now focus very briefly on the military police and direct your attention to Exhibit 457. Exhibit 457 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where is it? Is it in the second binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It is in the second binder, Mr. President. I'm referring to tab 1 in that. As I indicated to Your Honours, this is a document that has been published by the military police administration for the Ministry of Defence of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. This document bears reading because, among other things, it goes into great detail about the structure, organisation and the reorganisation of the military police in Central Bosnia. As I said, there are a number of articles in here which were submitted by various authors and were included in here. In respect of the structure of the 4th military police, in fact, the HVO military police, in HVO-controlled areas, I would direct your attention to the article that is written by Pavo Loncar. That should be the first major article that's contained in this. I won't direct you to specific passages in that at this point, but I can tell you that if there's any question about the structure of the HVO military police, you may find answers that are contained in that particular article. What I'm more interested in directing your attention to is portions of Mr. Loncar's article, and Mr. Loncar is a high ranking officer in the military police administration in Mostar. If I could direct your attention to page 15 of the English version and page 8 of the French version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, are we still in that document or are we back now in the first binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We're in the second binder, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. What can be given to the interpreters? Can we give them the whole binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I think not, Mr. President. I will speak very slowly. First of all, let me refer Your Honours to the issue of command of the military police units. Let me direct your attention once again to pages 14 and 15 of the English translation and page 8 of the French translation. Let me quote then from the English translation found at pages 14 and 15. This is from the article of Pavo Loncar: "With regard to the division of authority in the military police, the 1st MP Battalion was directly linked to the chief of the Administration, on whose orders it operated throughout the HZ HB. The 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th MP Battalions had authority over all military police affairs in their operative zones. In their daily tasks, commanders of the operative zone battalions were directly subordinate to the commander of the operative zone." And the paragraph goes on. Now, to illustrate what kind of units the military police units were, Mr. President, let me direct your attention to, first of all, an article that was written by Pasko Ljubicic. Unfortunately, there's not a French translation of this article, but on the English translation at pages 64 through 66, Mr. Ljubicic describes -- first of all, at page 65, I should say, he describes that he was appointed to be the commander of the 4th military police battalion. Then at page 65, let me read the following. There's no French translation of this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what that English translation or version is? Who was it authored by?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's authored by Pasko Ljubicic who was the commander of the 4th military police battalion, and at page 65 of the English translation, I'm reading from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- last part of the paragraph that appears at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I've got it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I quote: "When speaking about the activities and tasks of the MP, I was expressing my personal opinion, but I believe that the MP in Central Bosnia was the most organised force in the defence of those areas, made great sacrifices and, at times, played a decisive role in the defence of the area. Here, I can mention Grbavica, Simino Selo, Zabrde, Kruscica, Ahmici and several other places which I am sure and can prove that they were successfully protected through the involvement of the MP." Then I would like to go down two paragraphs further toward the middle of the page, and I would like to read another portion. He's describing why so many numbers of military police have been killed. I will pick up the paragraph mid-paragraph: "They were wounded and killed because they were always sent to the most difficult places and because they spent most of the time on the frontlines carrying out combat assignments. I claim that the MP in Central Bosnia was a military police least of all and had transformed itself into a combat unit." Then if I could direct your attention to page 15 of the English translation and page 8 of the French translation, I'm reading from the second paragraph of the English translation found at page 15 starting at the second sentence: "In these battles, the MP carried out" -- I'm sorry, Mr. President, this is found at page 9 of the French translation. If I said page 8 previously, I may have misspoken. Now I'll quote the English translation: "In these battles, the MP carried out all tasks assigned to it and proved to be an indispensable part of the HVO forces involved, especially in street battles, offensives and the liberation of some areas. Their participation in the heaviest fighting of this conflict resulted in a considerable number of casualties among Military Police members." In the same article by Pavo Loncar - if I could direct your attention to page 17 of the English translation and page 12 of the French translation - I'm reading slightly below midway through the page. Let me start with the paragraph: "At that time, there was heavy fighting between the HVO and ABH in all areas of the HZ HB except in the Posavina region. The Military Police participated in all combat operations both to defend and liberate occupied parts of the territory. In addition to the light assault battalions, the general battalions of the Military Police also contributed fully. Thus, the entire Military Police was engaged in combat operations, thereby also representing the most mobile component of all units of the HVO." As I say, Mr. President and Your Honours, this whole article, this whole set of articles, is well worth reading and will put into perspective for Your Honours the structure, the purpose, and the command of the HVO military police in Central Bosnia. Now, Mr. President, I would like to turn to a series of orders which will be found starting with tab 45 and ending with tab 54. I would direct your attention, first of all, to tab 45. This is an order, Mr. President, that has been issued by Colonel Blaskic. It is dated the 17th of April and it indicates that it was issued at 23.45 hours. It was issued, the addressee is the Ban Jelacic Brigade command in Kiseljak. If I may direct your attention to paragraph 1, there's a definition of the enemy. "1) Enemy: Continues to massacre Croats in Zenica where Muslim forces are using tanks to fire at people, mostly women and children. All of today's attacks have been repelled. The enemy has been totally crushed and it is compelled to continually bring in fresh forces." Paragraph 2, "Your assignment." Paragraph 2.2, "Using all available artillery, carry out fire preparations for the attack from the VU. Capture Gomionica and Svinjarevo through systematic targeting (60, 82 and 120 mm MB)."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down a little bit? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "Afterwards, regroup forces and carry out artillery preparations for launching an attack on and the capture of Bilalovac. 3) Fojnica must secure your left flank and launch an attack on Dusina or a breakthrough towards Sebisic." I direct your attention then to paragraph 9 which indicates, "Maintain a sense of historic responsibility," and paragraph 10 is the order "Begin the operation on 18 April 1993 at 0530 hours." Now, approximately two hours later, according to the next document which is found at tab 46, Colonel Blaskic issued another order. This order, dated the 18th of April, 1993 at 01.40 hours, is addressed to the commander of the Fojnica HVO battalion. Now, under "1) The Enemy," it says as follows and I'll read that: "The Enemy: Attacks on HVO units continue unabated along the entire Lasva Valley and their purpose is the full ethnic cleansing of Croats from the area and the destruction of all institutions of the HVO. The enemy has demonstrated its brutality and its aggressive behaviour in Zenica because of which the Croatian inhabitants have been moving out in large numbers. Attacks so far by the enemy have been repelled in the area of the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca, forcing it to bring in fresh forces from the region of Kakanj, Visoko, Zenica, and other Muslim locations in order to achieve its objectives. A large number of forces also from your area have been engaged for offensive operations against the Croatian people in the areas of Jablanica and Konjic municipalities. 2) Your Unit's Assignment is the following: Regroup the forces of your," and then there's a question mark as to whether this says "battalion," "... and carry out a combat operation on the village of Dusina or a breakthrough in the direction of the Busovaca stables and link up with forces defending Sebesic." I won't read the rest of it but it's a combat order. Now, I direct your attention then to paragraph 5 which says: "Implementation of this assignment must begin tomorrow after an assessment has been made." That was issued on the 18th of April, 1993. If I can now turn Your Honours' attention to tab 47, which is a command issued by Colonel Blaskic. There is no time given. This is a command for a cease-fire on the basis of orders given to him by the HVO head of staff on the 18th of April, and there's a particular order number identified. The addressees in this particular command are indicated as commanders of all HVO units, UNPROFOR, ECMM, and the 3rd Corps. This calls, in paragraph 1, for combat operations to stop immediately. Paragraph 4 commands that relevant data about the actors of the conflict, the causes of banishing people, murdering civilians and soldiers, burning houses and other buildings be gathered. So that's on the 18th of April, 1993. On the 19th of April, if we turn to tab 48, Colonel Blaskic issues a reminder to the commander of the Fojnica battalion, personally. This was issued at 18.00 hours, and I will read a part of the first paragraph: "I call your attention to your duty to execute and comply with the orders issued by the commander of the Kiseljak Ban Jelacic Brigade. Otherwise, you will be replaced and will be held responsible in compliance with the regulations of the HZ HB and in line with military discipline." Forty-five minutes later, Mr. President, if we turn to tab 49, forty-five minutes later, Colonel Blaskic issues an order to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak. This is dated the 19th of April, 1993 at 18.45 hours. I direct your attention to paragraph 1, "You must go on because the Croatian people have no other choice for the time being." Paragraph 3 of that same order, "Attack in groups and only diagonally from Kocatale and Sikulja." Lastly, I direct your attention to paragraph 5 which reads as follows: "The future of all Croats in Busovaca, Travnik, Vitez, and Novi Travnik depends upon your success, whereas in Zenica," words illegible, apparently, follow that, "... in any concentration camp, particularly in Gornja Zenica, where our people who fled from the centre of Zenica are being slaughtered even today. There is a massacre." Now, Mr. President, if we turn to tab 50, this is an order that is issued on the 19th of April at 21.40 hours to the Ban Jelacic Brigade command in Kiseljak. It is issued by Colonel Blaskic. It says in paragraph 1, "You must take Gomionica tonight or in the early morning." I won't read further. Paragraph 3, I'll read the first two sentences of paragraph 3, "At the moment, the Croatian people of Zenica are going through the most critical period. They are literally being slaughtered." Paragraph 4 I invite your attention to, because in that Colonel Blaskic states: "Generally, the situation is under control at all positions and we have informed the leadership of the HZ HB of everything. We are in constant contact with the leadership." Turning to the next document, which is document 51, this is an order from Colonel Blaskic on the 20th of April, 1993 at 11.15 hours, and it's an order for a bilateral cease-fire. It is the result, Colonel Blaskic issuing this order, apparently the result of a joint order that he has received from the HVO and the ABiH chiefs of staff regarding this particular cease-fire. He instructs, in paragraph 5, that the order for cease-fire will go into effect at 19.00 hours on that very same date, the 20th of April, 1993. Five minutes later, Mr. President, if you turn to tab 52, this is a command by Colonel Blaskic dismissing Mr. Stjepan Tuka, who is the commander of the battalion in Fojnica, "because of his failure to carry out his combat missions." If we turn to the next item, 53, which is dated the 20th of April, the same day that Commander Tuka receives notice that he is going to be dismissed, 53 is a communication to the Ban Jelacic brigade from Commander Tuka. In that, he acknowledges receipt of the previous order issued by Colonel Blaskic dismissing him. Lastly, in this series, Mr. President and Your Honours, I turn to tab 54, which is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 20th of April, 1993 subordinating the Fojnica 3rd Battalion to a brigade in Busovaca and under the command of the Kiseljak Ban Jelacic Brigade commander. That is a series of interesting orders, Mr. President, in or around the time of the 17th through the 20th of April that we would like to invite your attention to. Next, Mr. President, I would like to turn to items 55 through 60 that deal with Ahmici. Now, very briefly, item 55 I've previously described in 47. There is no need to repeat it, other than to identify this as a command that was given to stop combat operations. Item 56 is of interest because item 56 is a communiqué to Colonel Blaskic from Colonel Robert Stewart of the BRITBAT division commander, and it is direct notice to Colonel Blaskic that an atrocity has occurred in Ahmici. It is dated the 22nd of April, and it is captioned "Investigation of Atrocity." "1) At 14.00 hours today I visited the village of Ahmici. 2) In one house, I discovered the bodies of a man and a boy at the front entrance. Both bodies were burnt beyond recognition. In the cellar, I found the bodies of what may have been a mother and at least five children. Again, the bodies were burnt beyond recognition, and it was clear from the angle of the heads that at least two had died in agony. 3) Whoever has done this is guilty and must be punished. No atrocity, wherever it occurs, is acceptable. 4) I urgently request your help in order to investigate the sacking of this village." Now, if we turn to tab 57, there is a reply by Colonel Blaskic to Colonel Stewart. It is dated the following day, the 23rd of April, 1993. I direct your attention to the first paragraph wherein Colonel Blaskic states: "I'm ready to send immediately the investigating commission," and apparently it's cut off but it must mean "to," and then it says, "... village of Ahmici as well as to all other places who need investigated," part of this document has been cut off on the right-hand side. So it sounds like it's not properly being read, but I will read it as the text appears. Let me start again. "I am ready to send immediately the investigating commission, the village of Ahmici as well as to all other places that need investigated because of gathering facts about all the innocent victims this conflict." Now if we turn to the next item, 58. Fifty-eight is a very interesting document because 58 is a document recounting Colonel Blaskic's meeting with Colonel Stewart of the 24th of April, 1993. Now, first off, of interest, this document was addressed to the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, to the head of the Herceg-Bosna Defence Department, and to the HVO main headquarters chief. It is an information document about a discussion with Colonel Stewart that was held on the 24th of April, 1993. The subject of this particular meeting was: "The massacre of Muslim people in the village of Ahmici, Vitez municipality, and the visit of the Security Council delegation today, 24 April, 1993." What is interesting is there is -- first, this document is divided into first what was said by Colonel Stewart apparently to Colonel Blaskic, because that is the way he is recounting it to the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna. Included in this, Mr. President -- I won't read the whole document -- but is that Ahmici is in the -- Colonel Stewart told Colonel Blaskic that Ahmici was in the area, HVO area of responsibility, that no one has taken responsibility and no commission has been formed, and that the HVO wants to destroy Muslims. Colonel Stewart then makes the following comment: "I think that Mr. Mate Boban should have been in Vitez today." Bullet points follow then. Bullet 1: "Indicate that the reporting is extremely biased." Bullet point 2: "Point out the sufferings of the Rajic family." Bullet point 3: "Point out the suffering of the 2nd HVO Zenista Brigade and the Croats of Zenica." Next: "Stress the massacre of the Rajic family." Next: "To talk about the extremely one-sided emphasis on the suffering of only one people, expressing the suspicion that journalists are being paid to report events untruthfully." Next: "The shelling of Zenica. Only Croatian territory. The shelling of Kiseljak, et cetera." Next: "Classical terrorist actions against the commanding cadre that are being cancelled by all media organisations and others." The next document, Mr. President, and there is no reference in this document to any inquiry or any investigation or commission, the next document, Mr. President, I direct your attention to, is found at tab 59, and this is an order by Colonel Blaskic dated the 10th of May, 1993, 17.05 hours. The addressees are not evident because those have been blacked out. This is the form in which we received this document. This says: "For several days, various rumours have been circulating in the public ..." First of all, let me just add one thing, Mr. President. As I say, this is dated the 10th of May, so this is many days after Colonel Stewart has advised Colonel Blaskic of the atrocity in Ahmici. I am going to read the text of what is in this order: "For several days, various rumours have been circulating in the public regarding events in the village of Ahmici since 14 May, 1993 --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you mind slowing down for the interpreters? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: "-- and the civilian casualties there. In order to be able to analyse the events, establish the facts of the case, and implement the order of the HVO chief of staff, I hereby issue the following." So you can see that Colonel Blaskic is initiating an inquiry based on an order from the Croatian chief of staff, and then he orders in this, that information be collected, that a report be prepared, and that the deadline for the submission of that particular report is the 25th of May, 1993. Mr. President, I now turn to tab 60, the last document in the series of exhibits, only to show for Your Honours a contrasting approach that was taken by the HVO in respect of events that they considered to be important to them, and this is 17th of April, 1993 information that was conveyed to the ICRC, to the European Community, and to UNPROFOR, and it concerns the massacre of civilians in Kuber. This document indicates that, based on the information that the information office of the Central Bosnia operation zone had received on the 17th of April, that Muslim extremists are killing the civilian population in the villages of Jelinac and Putis in the Kuber, and they implore the addressees to exert their influence and do anything they can to prevent these massacres from taking place. Furthermore, Mr. President, the HVO suggest that they deploy -- that the addressees deploy their forces to that location to investigate the facts at the scene of the massacre, because according to unofficial information, approximately 60 civilians had been massacred at that location. Your Honours have heard evidence from other witnesses about the events that took place in these villages. That concludes that section of interesting documents on Ahmici, and I would like to turn, just direct Your Honours' attention -- I won't quote from these particular documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we might have a break, a 20-minute break, before turning to the next documents. Let me call your attention to this: Let's think of tomorrow, about the way we are going to organise our working day tomorrow. If you have a witness, he should be called tomorrow because, as you know, the Bench will be somewhat different as of Monday, we are going to have a different composition, so we shouldn't have a witness starting with one Bench and not finishing with the same Bench. Should you have a witness tomorrow, I think that we should finish with that witness tomorrow. As of Friday -- I have been corrected by my colleague -- as of Friday, we are having a different composition, and we have got your agreement, the agreement of the Defence, due to the exceptional circumstances, just think of it, and I'm sure we can tackle that as soon as we resume. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused come in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Let me now direct your attention to the orders that are found in tabs 61 through 68. I will not refer to any of them specifically but merely point out to Your Honours that these address the power and authority of Colonel Blaskic to appoint and to dismiss his subordinates, and they are a series of orders wherein Colonel Blaskic appoints and dismisses particular named individuals at various locations over a considerable period of time. Turning your attention to tabs 69 through 77, these items address a host of issues, particularly Colonel Blaskic's wide-ranging ability to arrest, to punish, and to sentence individuals under his command, and if I could merely note for Your Honours the items that are found in tabs 69 and 70, both of which are orders by Colonel Blaskic pursuant to the relevant articles relating to military discipline, imposing sentences in military prison on individuals. In tab 69, he imposes a sentence of 60 days on an individual for a particular violation; and at tab 70, the order imposes a sentence of 30 days on an individual. Tabs 71 and 72 are introduced to illustrate that the authority of subcommanders to discipline subordinates of theirs, and 71 and 72 are Defence Exhibits, Defence Exhibit 90 and Defence Exhibit 91, wherein a military police company commander imposes discipline on a subordinate for violations which are described in each of those particular orders. Tab number 73 is a communiqué that was issued by the information office of the Central Bosnia operation zone, and it refers to sentences of the Travnik District Military Court, which is based in Vitez, being imposed on named individuals for criminal violations. In one case, an eight-month suspended sentence for aggravated robbery, and in another case, a shorter suspended sentence for aggravated robbery. Now I would like to direct your attention briefly to tab number 74, which is a communication of Colonel Blaskic. I might indicate for the record that the index is wrong. It says 1993. The index should say 24 October, 1992. This is a communication of Colonel Blaskic, and I quote: "Mensud Alic, Major in the JNA, is currently in Trogir. If he should take the road to Travnik, arrest him, and if he resists, execute him." Item number 75 is an order of Colonel Blaskic to arrest a particular individual and take him to prison and to prepare the necessary documents and evidence to support specific charges that have been laid against him. Tab 76 is another order by Colonel Blaskic to arrest a particular soldier, and tab 77, now at the outer end of the last in this series, 11 October of 1993, is an order by Colonel Blaskic identifying disciplinary measures to be taken against soldiers and their superiors who abandon the defence lines, and I direct your attention to paragraph 1 of that particular item. First of all, it's addressed to various commanders, and I point out the addressees include independent units as well, and I will read now from the order: "(1) Undertake the following disciplinary measures against any soldier and their immediate commander who desert defence lines: (a) execution of the unit/soldier; (b) unit commanders will be declared traitors of the nation and given the most severe sentence of death by firing squad in front of the unit." So that, Mr. President, concludes this series of orders intended to illustrate the wide-ranging authorities of Colonel Blaskic in respect of sentencing, arresting, investigating, et cetera. Now if I could turn your attention to the items found in tabs 78 to tab 92, these specific items deal with communications in the Central Bosnia operation zone and these cover a wide range of time, starting in September of '92 and ending in June of 1993. If I could direct your attention to 78, which is issued by Colonel Blaskic on the 1st of September, 1992, and I point out that this is a request for certain information and it is directed to the HVO municipal headquarters in 21 different municipalities in Central Bosnia. Now, if Your Honours would turn to tab 79, this is a document which identifies tasks for the Central Bosnia operation zone command headquarters, and it is dated the 20th of September, 1992. If I can direct Your Honours to paragraph 17 of that particular document? In paragraph 17, and I quote: "Organise and put into use a full communications centre, find the means for preparing radio-paket-vezas, and obtain and begin operating a fax at this headquarters responsible for the task chief of communications, deadline 21 to 30 September, 1992." Now, in tab 81 -- I'm sorry, let me go to tab 80. This is a document that has been previously discussed as item number 2, and this is the order that Colonel Blaskic sent out to form special units for combat operations. I point out to Your Honours paragraph 2 in that specific order that indicates "that units for assault operations must be equipped with communications devices." Then, Mr. President and Your Honours, if I can turn to tab 81 and direct your attention to communications again in that particular area? This is the 7th of October, 1992, and it's another order from Colonel Blaskic, and it's directed to the commanders of 14 municipal headquarters in 14 different municipalities, I should say. Now, what's interesting about this is paragraph 2, which indicates that on that very same day by 4.00, the commanders in five of those municipalities had to reply to Colonel Blaskic. Item number 82 in this exhibit is of interest, Mr. President. First of all, it's an order for combat readiness issued by Milvoj Petkovic, who is a chief of staff of the HVO, and it was issued on the 16th of December, 1992, and it indicates a level of communication in that particular area of operation. It indicates on paragraph 6, and I quote: "Until further notice, submit a written report twice a day (at 0800 and at 1800 hours). Submit special reports as needed." Now, this, Mr. President and Your Honours, is an order that General Petkovic issued from Mostar, and he is requesting that he be apprised from the Central Bosnia operation zone twice a day of a response. The other interesting feature about this particular order is that it is marked "Coded." Now, item number 83 again is an item from General Petkovic, and again it is marked "Coded," and it has in it a request in item number 7 to submit regular and emergency reports on the situation on the ground, again directing copies to the Vitez municipality and other municipalities to communicate back to Mostar. Item number 84, dated January the 15th, 1993, is an order from General Petkovic once again, and his order, he orders all units of the HVO -- I'm sorry. In this particular order, which refers to the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, he requests in item number 9 that the people who are in receipt of this order should report on the implementation of this particular order every eight hours. I would like to focus your attention on the next two orders in conjunction with each other, 85 and 86. Item number 85, first of all, let me say, is issued January the 16th, 1993. The index is wrong. It has dropped the number 9 on the date. It should read "16th January, 1993," and it was issued by Colonel Blaskic at 11.40 hours. There's an order number that is given, 184-93, and it's issued to all formations in the Central Bosnia operation zone. Now, if you take a look at item number 86, 86 is another order issued on the same date by the commander of the Bobovac brigade in Vares. It is issued on the 16th of January at 22.30 hours. So shortly after Colonel Blaskic issued the order in item number 85, the commander of the Bobovac brigade in Vares, which was physically disconnected to the Kiseljak municipality, issues an order pursuant to Colonel Blaskic's order. Again, item number 87 merely indicates that General Petkovic, who issued an order on the 31st of January, 1993, requested a reply the next day, and he issued that particular order to the Central Bosnia operation zone and to other addressees throughout Central Bosnia. I turn your attention to item number 88. Again, this document is from an individual by the name of Kresimir Bozic and is dated 15 February, 1993 from Vares. It is a receipt and it indicates, and I quote: "We have received an order from the SBOZ," meaning Central Bosnia operation zone, "command through the packet network. A part of it is addressed to you and we will forward it to you so that you can file and implement it." I have already previously mentioned the dismissal, the order to dismiss Commander Tuca from his command in Fojnica and the reply of Commander Tuca. I mentioned those previously in items 52 and 53, but those two orders viewed together also indicate that on the 20th of April when, the evidence has shown in this case, combat operations were extremely intense, an order was issued by Colonel Blaskic from his headquarters in Vitez to an area that was physically disconnected to his headquarters in Fojnica. In conjunction with these two orders, it is clear that the order was issued, and on the same day it was received and acted upon by Commander Tuca in the area of Fojnica. Item number 91 I direct your attention to because, although it's the same item that has been previously discussed, item 50, it is a communication from Colonel Blaskic on the 19th of April, 1993 to the Ban Jelacic brigade command in Kiseljak. What is interesting about this are the two features found one in item number 4 indicating that Colonel Blaskic had informed the leadership of Herceg-Bosna of the situation, and quote: "We are in constant contact with the leadership." The other interesting feature about this particular document is a hand-written notation in the upper right-hand corner of this document that indicates quote: "Arrived from Vitez on 19 April, 1993 at 23.35 hours, received by Mario B." So this indicates that it was received in Kiseljak shortly after its transmission from Vitez at 21.40 hours. "Mario B," I don't know who the "B" is, but the court has heard evidence that an individual by the name of Mario Bradara was the deputy commander of the Ban Jelacic brigade in Kiseljak. Lastly, in this particular sequence, I refer Your Honours' attention to item number 93. It is an order from Colonel Blaskic. It is dated the 1st of June, 1993 at 09.00 hours, and I direct your attention to item number 3 which says, "Have courier and communications system prepared for rapid and effective summoning of manpower." That concludes these series of documents on communication, and I would like to now turn to the documents that are contained in items 93 to 103 which deal with propaganda and disinformation. I will start by directing Your Honours' attention to item number 93, which is an order issued by Colonel Blaskic as the commander of the Central Bosnia operation zone and by Dario Kordic as the Vice-President of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Dario Kordic identifies himself as "colonel" in that particular document. Let me refer to paragraph 5 which is entitled "Information and Propaganda Activity." This is dated the 15th of June, 1992. Let me read item 5. "Information and Propaganda Activity. Impress upon the people and the soldiers the brutality of the aggression of the Muslim armed forces and that the only way to prevent a massacre is to fight the enemy and to protect our people and pledge that we will eventually return to our territory." Let me turn to item number 94, which is issued approximately three weeks later on the 4th of July, 1992. It's an order issued by Colonel Blaskic. If I can direct Your Honours' attention to paragraph 6 which I quote: "Intensify propaganda activities in order to boost morale and create a sense of insecurity in the enemy. Officer in Charge: Operative Zone Commanders. Method: Follow the instructions. Deadline: 10 July, 1992." Now, I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to a very important document which is item number 95 - I'll come back to this particular document later - but this is a document that is excerpts of a meeting of the Croatian Defence Councils in the municipalities of Central Bosnia, and it is signed by Herceg-Bosna HVO Secretary, Ignac Kostroman; Deputy President of the HVO government, Anto Valenta; and Deputy President of the HVO Herceg-Bosna, Dario Kordic. You will notice in this particular document that the attendees include Colonel Blaskic, and on the first page of that document, Colonel Blaskic is identified as being one of four members of the working presidency, along with Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, and Ignac Kostroman. In this document, there is a section under "Observations," towards the end of this document, and it says under "Observations noted in all municipalities: There has to be strong HVO propaganda everywhere." Now, let me go ahead to documents 98 and 99. These documents somewhat echo one another. The first document, which is found at 99, is an appeal for help for the Croats of Zenica. It is dated 17th of April, 1993, and it is signed by the Minister of Defence Ante Puljic; Secretary-General of Herceg-Bosna, Ignac Kostroman; and Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, Dario Kordic. In this document addressed to UNPROFOR, BRITBAT commander Colonel Stewart, ECMM, Mr. Thebaud, and ICRC, these three political leaders implore the addressees to do all that is possible to protect the Croats in Zenica who, they allege, are being subjected to tank attacks. They allege that the mujahadeen forces have started using tanks against women and children. In item number 99, which is entitled "Protest," it is a protest of Colonel Blaskic to UNPROFOR and ECMM the following day. In this document, and I quote, Colonel Blaskic says as follows: "In their severe attacks on the Croatian villages of Zenica municipality, Muslim forces are using all their bestiality and cruelty as well as their evident wish of destroying all that is Croatian. In the city itself, the arresting, harassing and the robbing of civilian women and children is going on for a long time now. The men arrested are thrown under tanks ..." and it goes on. It is an echo of the previous appeal that was sent by Dario Kordic, Ignac Kostroman, and Mr. Puljic that is described in item number 98. In the area of disinformation, Mr. President, I direct your attention to a very interesting document and Your Honours' attention also to this document found at tab 100. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We were trying to find a procedure which is not to be found in the rules to make you understand that you were just about to lose a very essential part of your clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab number 100 is a very interesting item. It is a letter addressed to the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zenica. It is dated the 16th of April, 1993. It indicates, and I will quote it, I'll quote a portion of it: "This morning, your forces launched an attack on the Central Bosnia operation zone command. We are surprised and outraged by such an act, on top of everything else that your members have recently done. We do not want conflict, but this morning we were forced to respond to the attack launched by your members." In the area of propaganda as well, Mr. President, I have previously identified a document, item number 58, which was the report of Colonel Blaskic to the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna and other superiors indicating Colonel Blaskic's meeting with Colonel Stewart that was held on the 24th of April, 1993. I specifically direct Your Honours' attention to those portions starting with the sentence, "I think that Mate Boban should have been in Vitez today." He goes on to explain why, after being apprised of the massacres at Ahmici, he thought Mr. Boban should have been present. If I can direct your attention to item number 102, an item that has been previously discussed under tab 32 which is the special report on the situation in Central Bosnia operation zone. It was addressed by Colonel Blaskic on the 7th of May, 1993 to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, that would be Mate Boban; the head of the Defence department of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna; the chief of the main headquarters of the HVO in Mostar. I would like to direct Your Honours' attention to the last page, the last sentence in that particular document, and I will quote: "I would like to thank you personally and on behalf of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone Command for everything you have done so far in terms of logistics and propaganda support." I will not touch upon the remaining document in this particular set of documents. Instead, Mr. President, I would like to turn very, very briefly to documents 104 to 108. These documents are self-explanatory. They describe training that was available to various elements in the HVO. The only particular document I would like to address Your Honours' attention to is in 106. This is an order by Colonel Blaskic dated the 20th of September, 1992. Under item number 3, which was identified by Colonel Blaskic as a task of the HVO Central Bosnia operation zone command headquarters, under 3: "The training of new recruits who have not served in the JN (Yugoslav Army) is to be basic and specific (recruit all able-bodied men over 18). Responsible for the task: ONO (Operations and Training Body). Deadline: 15-30 September 1992." The other documents, Mr. President, are self-explanatory and, Your Honours, they are self-explanatory. What I would like to do is return to the -- I'm having a little trouble with my cravat here today. I would like to turn Your Honours' attention to the item that's found in tab 109. That is the same document that I previously touched upon in 95. As I say, Mr. President and Your Honours, this is a document that is excerpts from a meeting of Croatian Defence Councils in the municipalities of Central Bosnia, and it was signed by Mr. Kostroman, Mr. Valenta, and Mr. Kordic. It indicates that Colonel Blaskic attended, took part in the discussion, and was a member of the working presidency, along with Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, and Ignac Kostroman. There's a section of this particular document dealing with observations noted in all the municipalities. In this particular section, let me just quote some of the relevant portions of that. I quoted one portion that indicates that there has to be strong HVO propaganda everywhere, but let me quote some of the other portions to Your Honours. "In Central Bosnia, the HOS have almost completely put themselves under the command of the HVO. In many areas, the HOS has been dissolved and its members have joined the HVO." Another observation in this was as follows: "New refugees are arriving almost daily, especially Muslims. This could disturb the ethnic balance in our areas. The police should be such that our municipalities serve as transit points for Muslim refugees who should be directed to Muslim municipalities." Another quotation is as follows: "Reception centres for refugees which are planned by the government in Sarajevo on Croatian territories are not acceptable to the Croatian population because that would mean a disruption of the ethnic balance." Another quote found in there is as follows: "Exiled B and H government and its bodies with pro-Muslim policies are undesirable on our territory, and their possible activity, contrary to the principles of HDZ bodies, shall not be tolerated." Another portion of this document I will read: "There is no Bosnian language, and it is an insult to the Croatians when anyone tries to make the Croatian language into some kind of a Bosnian language." Another portion: "Military HVO authorities are asked to speed up the process of making the military formations more professional, of introducing order in military circles, and making the military police professional. They should also put an end to war profiteers." Lastly, and I quote: "HVO military bodies for Central Bosnia shall produce Defence plans against possible attack by Islamic fundamentalist mujehadeen forces and introduce military discipline and order in the military formations." Now, I have taken selected quotes from this particular document. My suggestion, Your Honours, is to read the document in total to get a flavour of this particular document. I don't want to take anything out of context, and I think Your Honours can see this document in its totality and it will be of interest. I'm turning to these miscellaneous documents now -- that was one of them, Mr. President. Let me turn to another miscellaneous document which is found at tab 110, and this is an undated document, but there is a receipt apparently at the bottom indicating 24 with a possibility of it being October of 1992. This is a document, and it was transmitted by the Vice-President of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Dario Kordic, and transmitted by the commander of the Central Bosnia operative headquarters, Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, and it indicates information about the movement of Muslim forces. If we turn next to document 111, this is a document, Mr. President and Your Honours, which is dated the 25th of May, 1993, it is a request by Colonel Blaskic, as the commander of the Central Bosnia operation zone, and by Anto Valenta, HVO Herceg-Bosna Vice-President. It is addressed to UNPROFOR, to UNHCR, and to ECMM. It is in two variations, one of which is -- I'm sorry. There is a request in this that is in the original in English, and it has two stamps, one from Colonel Blaskic and one from Anto Valenta, and it requests the reduction of Muslim interpreters working for international organisations in Central Bosnia. I can turn Your Honours' attention to 112. This is a document addressed to ECMM, attention of Mr. Tiboa. I presume that is Mr. Thebault. It is dated the 26th of May, 1993, at 1800 hours, and it was sent by Colonel Blaskic, and it implores Colonel Blaskic to use -- I'm sorry. It implores Mr. Thebault to use his personal authority with 3rd Corps to implement agreements in line with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan. Document 113 is a document, information that was issued by Colonel Blaskic to ECMM, UNPROFOR, the Red Cross, and 3rd Corps on the 25th of April, 1993, and it indicates that Colonel Blaskic was aware that arresting civilians was in contravention of the Geneva accords. I direct Your Honours' attention to this document indicating that mudjehadeen forces had entered particular villages populated predominantly by Croats and taken away between 60 and 70 people and "the group comprises many elderly people, children and the sick who, under the Geneva Conventions, may not be subjected to such treatment." The last document under this miscellaneous category is document 114. It is an interesting document. The Court has heard testimony about helicopters in the recent days. This is a document that was issued by Colonel Blaskic. It is a request issued to the chief of staff of the HVO headquarters in Posusje, to Lieutenant General Anto Roso. Now, Posusje, as the Court may see from maps that have been introduced into evidence, is outside the Central Bosnia operation zone, it's near the Croatian border, it's near Grude. On the 4th of February, 1994, Colonel Blaskic, in item number 1, identifies items, and I quote: "As a matter of priority, send the required equipment by air." I direct your attention to a second item in that order: "Please send the automatic rifles and machine guns which I previously requested during my stay as they are absolutely necessary." That concludes, Mr. President and Your Honours, a review of some of these documents, and I would now ask that Exhibit 456 and 457 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any remarks, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No additional comments other than those previously made, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Turning to the registrar, the court deputy, we have ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 456.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And the second binder will have the number ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you want to make comments on the second binder, Mr. Harmon? We had commenced on the military police. It's up to you. You decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no additional comments on Exhibit 457. I have made my comments before. I was going to inform the Court that we do not have any additional witnesses today, nor do we for the remainder of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I see. So we're not going to have any witnesses tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we will resume our work on Tuesday -- I'm turning towards Mr. Fourmy. Are we starting again on Tuesday -- yes, that seems to be right -- for the last two days of the Prosecution case which will take place on Tuesday. What is the date on Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: On the 28th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And you will finish on Wednesday, the 29th, in the evening. Fine. Well, we will keep to this schedule, and we will then have the final stage of the Prosecution case unless -- I'm saying this because we are having a public hearing. There might be following hearings as a result of the subpoenas that were issued at some stage, and this may cause some changes in the schedule, but all this will be done in agreement with the Defence and in full compliance of the accusatorial procedure. Thank you very much. The proceedings shall adjourn. We shall resume on Tuesday, the 28th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
